title: station2radar: query-conditioned gaussian splatting for precipitation field
one_liner: QCGS turns sparse station readings plus satellite images into radar-like rain maps by rendering only the places you ask about instead of drawing the whole map every time.
lead: Rainfall mapping has three awkward data sources. Weather stations are accurate but sparse. Satellite images cover large areas but do not directly give rainfall at the ground. Radar provides the best rain field, but radar coverage is expensive and incomplete. This paper builds a system that fuses station readings with satellite imagery to generate a radar-like rain field. The system renders only queried rain regions, so it preserves sharp structure while avoiding work in dry areas where nothing needs to be drawn.

problem.h2: Rain data is either accurate, sparse, or incomplete
paras: A weather station gives a trustworthy rainfall reading at one point. A satellite gives dense image coverage across a huge area, but it measures cloud appearance rather than rain at the ground. Radar gives the closest thing to a full rain map, yet many places do not have dense radar coverage because installation and upkeep are costly.

A naive system would spread station readings over a grid and smooth everything together with the satellite image. That blurs storm boundaries and wastes computation across dry regions, because the method treats empty land the same way it treats an active rain cell.

callout.html: We want radar-like rain fields without radar coverage, using sparse stations plus satellite context.

steps.text: Take point rainfall measurements from automatic weather stations and a matching satellite image for the same region and time.
A proposal network marks where strong rain structure probably exists.
An implicit network assigns size, weight, and shape values to each proposed location using both station and satellite context.
When the system is asked for rainfall over a region, it renders only the proposed locations that affect that query.
The selected local contributions are summed into a radar-like rainfall map.

paras: The paper changes the rendering strategy for rainfall fields. Instead of drawing the full map every time, it renders only the parts touched by the current rainfall query.

hidden.name: which local locations actually carry useful rainfall structure
paras: The system depends on a hidden map of support locations: small local places where rain structure should be represented explicitly. This quantity matters because most of the scene may be dry, while a few compact regions contain almost all of the useful detail.

The proposal network estimates this hidden support by combining station evidence with patterns in the satellite image. If it marks the right support locations, the renderer can stay focused and sharp because it spends its effort on wet regions instead of washing detail across the whole map.

heat.caption: Darker cells mark regions where the model believes explicit rainfall support is needed.

reads.html: This asks: 'Where is the rain structure important enough that we should explicitly draw it?'
The support set is produced by the radar point proposal network, which selects locations likely to contribute to the queried precipitation field.

paras: Full-map rendering spends equal attention on wet and dry areas. That is wasteful because rainfall is usually concentrated in limited regions. By first proposing support locations, the model knows where explicit local detail matters.

The renderer then answers only the region you ask for. That reduces computation because dry locations are skipped, and it preserves sharp storm boundaries because the method sums compact local contributions instead of spreading everything through a coarse grid. Station readings anchor the field to ground truth, while the satellite image supplies the broader spatial context that stations alone cannot provide.

This combination is especially useful outside radar coverage. The station data supplies trustworthy rainfall values, the satellite image provides spatial continuity, and query-conditioned rendering turns both into a flexible rain field that can be produced at different resolutions.

stages.s: render only locations touched by the query

math.words: Rainfall at a queried location is the sum of local weighted contributions from the proposed support points.
symbols: how much support point i contributes at location x
rainfall strength assigned to support point i

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose a queried location sits near three proposed support points.
Their contributions are 0.6, 0.3, and 0.1, and their rainfall strengths are 12, 8, and 2 mm/hr.
If the query moves into a dry area, the nearby weights drop toward zero, so the system returns little or no rain.

math.note: The whole method depends on learning good local weights and strengths, because those terms decide where rain appears and how sharp each boundary stays.

charts.title: Conventional gridded rainfall product
charts.note: Uniform gridding blurs precipitation structure and cannot focus work on queried wet regions.

charts.title: QCGS
charts.note: Selective rendering improves field quality because the method concentrates detail where rainfall actually exists.

items.html: If the proposal network fails to mark an active rain cell, the renderer cannot recover that structure later because it never draws from that missing support.
When very few stations exist in a region, the model must rely heavily on satellite appearance, which can confuse thick cloud with ground rainfall.
If station and satellite observations are misaligned in time, the fused field can shift storms into the wrong place because the data no longer describes the same weather state.

With aligned station and satellite inputs plus accurate support proposals, query-conditioned rendering improves rainfall mapping because it keeps detail in wet regions and avoids wasted work in dry ones.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Use a held-out region with station readings, satellite images, and radar targets. Build one baseline that spreads station data over a fixed grid and one QCGS-style model that proposes support points and answers regional queries. Evaluate both on several requested map windows and at multiple output resolutions.
demo.closing: The demo should show that selective rendering improves fidelity because it reconstructs active rain structure without spending equal effort on empty areas.
